summary: This Standards Track document points out limits of the dynamic IPv6 multicast address range from RFC 3307 and replaces it with a new IANA registry in the IPv6 Multicast Address Space group, with initial contents including a reduced allocation for MADCAP. It updates RFC 3307.

plainLanguage.summary: The old list of group-chat numbers is too small or awkward, so this builds a new, tidier list.

questions: what is the dynamic multicast group ids registry
what is the madcap group id range
subtitle: A new IANA registry carves up the dynamic IPv6 multicast group ID space so several allocation methods can coexist.

tldr.problem: RFC 3307 gave both server allocation and host allocation the same range of dynamic IPv6 multicast group IDs, so they could not coexist without risking collisions. That range also overlapped the Solicited-Node range.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 10028 replaces the allocation with a new IANA registry, Dynamic Multicast Group IDs, and fills it with separate ranges for MADCAP, host-allocated SSM groups, Private Use, Experimental Use and Solicited-Node addresses.
tldr.outcome: MADCAP gets a smaller range, and room is left unassigned for future allocation protocols. The RFC is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 3307.

facts.label: Group ID size
facts.value: 32 bits (lower bits of the IPv6 address)

today: RFC 10028 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2026. It updates RFC 3307 and has not been obsoleted or updated by a later RFC according to the unit metadata.

sections.title: The Problem With the Old Range
sections.content:
An IPv6 multicast address ends in a 32-bit group ID, which is mapped directly to the link layer. RFC 3307 hands out ranges of group ID values depending on how they are allocated, and describes two ways to assign them dynamically: server allocation and host allocation.

The trouble is that both approaches were given the same range of group IDs, so they cannot coexist without risking an address collision. The dynamic range also overlaps the range used for Solicited-Node multicast addresses, which is defined in RFC 4291. RFC 10019 discusses the problems of duplicate group IDs on a network.

Only one server allocation protocol had been defined at the time of writing, RFC 2730 (MADCAP). RFC 10019 advocates a decentralized, zero-configuration host allocation protocol. RFC 10028 therefore updates Section 4.3 of RFC 3307 so that several dynamic allocation protocols can share one network, and so the ranges live in a registry like protocol numbers do.
sections.plainLanguage: Two groups were told to use the same set of numbers for their rooms, so they could end up in the same room by accident. This RFC fixes that mix-up.

sections.title: Source-Specific Multicast and Why It Gets a Range
sections.content:
With Source-Specific Multicast (SSM), a host subscribes to a channel (S,G) and receives only packets for destination address G that come from source address S. RFC 4607 lists as a benefit that it avoids the need for inter-host coordination when choosing source-specific addresses.

That lowers the need for coordinated dynamic assignment of G. Several distinct hosts could use the same value for G, and traffic would still reach only the node that asked for the stream.

SSM is not universally supported, though. So this document defines a range of dynamic group IDs for environments that do support SSM.
sections.plainLanguage: If you only listen to one friend's walkie-talkie channel, it does not matter that other people picked the same channel number, because you only hear your friend.

sections.title: The Updated Group ID Ranges
sections.content:
Before this document, the allocations from RFC 3307 and RFC 4291 were summarized as two ranges. The range 0x80000000-0xFEFFFFFF was open to both server (MADCAP) and host allocation. The range 0xFF000000-0xFFFFFFFF was open to those two and was also used by Solicited-Node addresses.

The new "Dynamic Multicast Group IDs" registry replaces that with distinct ranges:

  • 0x80000000-0x8FFFFFFF: MADCAP
  • 0x90000000-0xEFFFFFFF: unassigned
  • 0xF0000000-0xFCFFFFFF: host allocation of SSM group addresses
  • 0xFD000000-0xFDFFFFFF: reserved for Private Use
  • 0xFE000000-0xFEFFFFFF: reserved for Experimental Use
  • 0xFF000000-0xFFFFFFFF: Solicited-Node multicast addresses

The Private Use range can serve isolated deployments, for example manual address allocation. The Experimental Use range may be used to try new dynamic allocation protocols, and there are no restrictions on experimental scope, so experiments may run over the open Internet. All remaining entries are reserved for future assignment as new protocols are developed.
sections.plainLanguage: The long list of numbers is cut into labeled blocks: one for the old system, one for a new kind of group, one for private use, one for experiments, and one for a special job. The rest stays empty until someone needs it.

sections.title: Impact on MADCAP Deployments
sections.content:
The change shrinks the range of group IDs available to MADCAP, but still leaves a sizable allocation. The RFC says that, at the time of writing, there is only one known implementation of MADCAP and no known large-scale deployments.

Any MADCAP implementations, known or otherwise, should be updated to the new range in Table 2 of the RFC. Existing MADCAP deployments should either use an updated implementation or operate in an environment without other IPv6 multicast address allocation protocols.
sections.plainLanguage: The old system now gets a smaller set of rooms. Anyone still using it should switch to the new set or make sure nobody else is using the same building.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC adds nothing new here. It states that it does not expand on any security considerations beyond what is discussed in RFC 3307 and RFC 2908.
sections.plainLanguage: This change only reorganizes a list, so it brings no new safety worries beyond the ones already written down.

sections.title: The New IANA Registry
sections.content:
IANA has created the "Dynamic Multicast Group IDs" registry in the "IPv6 Multicast Address Space" registry group. Updating it requires the "Standards Action" registration policy. Each entry has three fields: a Range of 32-bit values in hexadecimal within 0x80000000 to 0xFFFFFFFF, a Description, and a Reference. The registry starts with the entries described above and cites both RFC 3307 and this document.

IANA also updated the entry for FF3X:0:0:0:0:0:8000:0-FF3X:0:0:0:0:0:FFFF:FFFF in the "Unicast-based (Including SSM) Multicast Group IDs" registry. It now says the range uses dynamic assignment according to the protocols in the new registry, and its reference points to this document.
sections.plainLanguage: A keeper of the list, IANA, now has a new page for these room numbers. Changing it needs a formal standards decision, and the old page now points to the new one.
